Title: [Effects of Tongqiao Huoxue Decoction on cognitive dysfunction and expression of insulin signaling pathway-related proteins in rats with Alzheimer's disease].
Original_Abstract: To investigate the effects of Tongqiao Huoxue Decoction(TQHX) on cognitive dysfunction and the expression of insulin signaling pathway-related proteins in rats with Alzheimer's disease(AD), Sprague-Dawley(SD) rats were randomly divided into a sham-operated group, an AD group, a low-dose TQHX group, a medium-dose TQHX group, a high-dose TQHX group, and a positive control group. Following 28 days of treatment with TQHX or the positive control drug memantine, the homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance(HOMA-IR) was determined. Cognitive function was evaluated using the Morris water maze. Hematoxylin-eosin(HE) staining and silver staining were performed to examine neuronal and synaptic morphology in the hippocampal CA1 region, and neuronal regeneration was assessed by immunofluorescence staining for doublecortin(DCX). The mitochondrial membrane potential(MMP) of brain tissue cells was measured using the JC-1 fluorescent probe, and adenosine triphosphate(ATP) levels were determined. The content of Aβ in brain tissue and the levels of malondialdehyde(MDA) and superoxide dismutase(SOD) were measured. Serum inflammatory cytokine levels were determined by ELISA. The expression of insulin signaling pathway-related proteins in brain tissue was detected by Western blot. The results showed that, compared with the sham-operated group, the AD group exhibited significantly increased HOMA-IR, escape latency, Aβ content, MDA levels, tumor necrosis factor-α(TNF-α), interleukin(IL)-1β and IL-8 levels, as well as increased ratios of phosphorylated glycogen synthase kinase-3β(p-GSK-3β)/glycogen synthase kinase-3β(GSK-3β) and phosphorylated nuclear factor-κB p65(p-NF-κB p65)/nuclear factor-κB p65(NF-κB p65), whereas the number of platform crossings, hippocampal DCX-positive expression, neuronal dendritic spine density, MMP, ATP, SOD levels, insulin receptor(IR) protein expression, the ratio of phosphorylated insulin receptor substrate 1(p-IRS1)/insulin receptor substrate 1(IRS1), the ratio of phosphorylated phosphoinositide 3-kinase(p-PI3K)/phosphoinositide 3-kinase(PI3K), and the ratio of phosphorylated protein kinase B(p-AKT)/protein kinase B(AKT) were significantly decreased. Compared with the AD group, all TQHX treatment groups and the positive control group showed decreased HOMA-IR, escape latency, Aβ content, MDA levels, TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-8 levels, and the p-GSK-3β/GSK-3β and p-NF-κB p65/NF-κB p65 ratios, whereas the number of platform crossings, hippocampal DCX-positive expression, neuronal dendritic spine density, MMP, ATP, SOD levels, IR protein expression, and the p-IRS1/IRS1, p-PI3K/PI3K, and p-AKT/AKT ratios were all increased. Moreover, these effects showed a dose-dependent trend among the TQHX groups. Compared with the high-dose TQHX group, no significant changes were observed in any of the measured parameters in the positive control group. In conclusion, TQHX improves cognitive dysfunction and insulin resistance in AD rats and upregulates the expression of insulin signaling pathway-related proteins.
AI_Summary: This study investigated whether a traditional herbal medicine, Tongqiao Huoxue Decoction (TQHX), could help treat Alzheimer's disease in rats. Researchers compared rats given different doses of the herbal medicine to those given a standard Alzheimer's drug. They found that TQHX significantly improved the rats' memory and learning abilities while protecting brain cells and promoting new nerve growth. The treatment also reduced brain inflammation and cellular damage, boosted brain energy, and restored healthy insulin signaling, which is typically disrupted by the disease. Higher doses of the herbal medicine worked just as effectively as the standard prescription drug, suggesting that TQHX may be a promising treatment for protecting brain health and reversing memory decline in Alzheimer's disease.

Title: [Jatrorrhizine alleviates hepatic endoplasmic reticulum stress, attenuates lipotoxicity, and improve insulin resistance by inhibiting UPR-mTOR-JNK axis].
Original_Abstract: This study aimed to explore the mechanism by which jatrorrhizine attenuates hepatic insulin resistance(IR) by regulating endoplasmic reticulum stress(ERS) in IR-HepG2 cells to improve glucose-lipid metabolism. A hepatic IR-HepG2 cell model was induced with 0.4 mmol·L~(-1) oleic acid(OA) for 24 h. The cells were then treated with 10, 20, and 40 μmol·L~(-1) jatrorrhizine for 36 h. Extracellular glucose content, cell viability and ATP content were detected. The effects of jatrorrhizine on lipid accumulation, mitochondrial integrity, apoptosis and reactive oxygen species(ROS) were observed. Proteins related to ERS, lipid synthesis/oxidative decomposition, mitochondrial/cell apoptosis and insulin signaling pathway were detected. Additionally, the IRE1α-specific inhibitor 4μ8C was added to examine extracellular glucose content, mitochondrial integrity, ROS, apoptosis and expression of related proteins. The results showed that jatrorrhizine inhibited the key unfolded protein response(UPR) pathways such as IRE1α/XBP1s and PERK/eIF2α/ATF4 of ERS, downregulated GRP78, and thereby alleviated excessive UPR activation. Moreover, jatrorrhizine up-regulated ATGL, PPARα and CPT1α to promote lipolysis and fatty acid β-oxidation, while down-regulating SREBP-1c and ChREBP to inhibit fatty acid synthesis, reduce intracellular lipid accumulation, and restore lipid homeostasis. Furthermore, jatrorrhizine not only up-regulated Pl3K p85 and p-Akt(Ser473) but also downregulated forkhead box O1(FOXO1),which activated the insulin signaling to reduce extracellular glucose. In addition, jatrorrhizine down-regulated p-JNK, CHOP, and Caspase-3, upregulated Bcl-2, reduced ROS and apoptosis, preserved mitochondrial structure, and increased ATP production. Following cotreatment with 4μ8C, the metabolic restoration effects of jatrorrhizine was reversed: GRP78 and ATF4 were compensatorily upregulated; p-JNK and CHOP expression rebounded; mitochondrial dysfunction was exacerbated; mTOR and S6K were abberantly activated; PI3K p85 and PPARα were downregulated; both lipid synthesis and oxidation were comprehensively blocked; and extracellular glucose content increased. These findings indicate that complete blockage of IRE1α/XBP1s compromised lipid oxidation, leading to lipotoxicity, impairs the cooperative balance upon UPR branches, triggers excessive compensatory activation of the PERK/ATF4 axis, and induces negative feedback inhibition on insulin signaling by mTOR, ultimately causing re-dysregulation of glucolipid metabolism in jatrorrhizine-treated IR-HepG2 cells. In conclusion, jatrorrhizine inhibits the UPR branches IRE1α/XBP1s and PERK/eIF2α/ATF4, downregulates the mTOR-FOXO1-JNK pro-apoptotic axis, activates PI3K/Akt signaling, promotes metabolic remodeling and energy expenditure, and alleviates lipotoxicity, thereby ameliorating hepatic IR in OA-induced IR-HepG2 cells.
AI_Summary: This study investigated how a natural plant compound called jatrorrhizine helps treat insulin resistance in liver cells overwhelmed by fat. Researchers found that jatrorrhizine reduces internal stress within the cells, which restores their ability to respond to insulin and effectively process sugar. It encourages liver cells to burn excess fat rather than store it, protects their energy-producing centers, and prevents cell death caused by stress. Ultimately, jatrorrhizine restores a healthy balance of sugar and fat in liver cells, making it a promising potential treatment for metabolic conditions like fatty liver disease and diabetes.

Title: From Obesity to Cancer Cachexia: PI3K/AKT/MTOR Signaling Across the Energy Balance Spectrum - A Scoping Review of Body Size, Composition, and Cancer Outcomes.
Original_Abstract: The PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling pathway is overactivated in cancer. Obesity is an established risk factor for several cancers, also variably associated with prognosis. Cancer cachexia is at the opposite end of the energy balance spectrum and is similarly linked to poor prognosis. Preclinical studies link obesity to activation of this pathway, whereas cachexia is associated with its suppression in skeletal muscle. However, human findings are inconsistent and often ignore the metabolic influence of body composition on MTOR activity. This scoping review summarizes how body size and composition-spanning obesity to cachexia-relate to PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling in cancer risk and outcomes. A systematic search in Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed through January 19, 2023, identified 6,285 studies; 139 met the inclusion criteria across 15 cancer types: gastrointestinal (n=48); gynecological (n=34); breast (n=30); male reproductive (n=7); lung (n=6); thyroid (n=6); renal (n=2); and skin (n=1) cancers, plus cachexia (n=5). Body size was associated with components and effectors of the PI3K/AKT/MTOR pathway, but findings were inconsistent, reflecting heterogeneity in cancer type, subtype, exposure and biomarker measurement, and unmeasured host factors. Insulin resistance and diabetes were more consistently associated with pathway markers than BMI. Across six studies, obesity and pathway markers often interacted, modifying each other's associations with cancer outcomes. Interventional studies of weight loss, metformin, and bariatric surgery reported changes in some tumor biomarkers, but none assessed cancer outcomes, limiting weight management guidance for patients with obesity. In cachexia, pathway analysis suggested increased catabolic and decreased anabolic muscle signaling, though findings varied by muscle site, and the effects of dietary interventions remain untested. Evidence predominantly relied on BMI rather than body composition components, leaving their relationship to PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling understudied. Standardized and longitudinal designs, body composition measurement, and assessment of metabolic status, diet, and physical activity are needed to advance precision nutritional oncology. REVIEW REGISTRATION: INPLASY202450036 https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2024.5.0036 STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: This scoping review is the first to comprehensively examine the associations between alterations in body size and composition-including both obesity and cancer-associated cachexia-and PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling in tumors, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle across cancer types in relation to clinical outcomes and patient survival. Findings reveal heterogeneity in study designs and highlight research gaps, including the need for more consistent measurement of body composition and incorporating host metabolic context, such as insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction. These efforts could harmonize results, improve comparability across studies, and advance nutritional and precision oncology.
AI_Summary: A large review of 139 studies examined how body size—ranging from obesity to severe weight and muscle loss—influences a key biological pathway that drives cancer growth. Researchers found that basic body weight measurements like BMI give inconsistent results when predicting cancer risk and patient outcomes. Instead, a person’s underlying metabolic health, such as having diabetes or insulin resistance, showed a much stronger and more consistent connection to these cancer-promoting signals. Furthermore, while weight-loss strategies and diabetes medications can alter these cellular signals, it remains unclear if they directly improve cancer survival. Ultimately, the review concludes that to improve personalized cancer care and nutrition, future research must look beyond simple body weight and focus on detailed body composition—specifically fat versus muscle mass—alongside overall metabolic health.

Title: Bergapten ameliorates type 2 diabetes mellitus by modulating hepatic glycogen metabolism, inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum stress: involvement of AKT signaling.
Original_Abstract: Bergapten (BP), derived from traditional Chinese medicinal herbs, exhibits therapeutic efficacy across multiple diseases. Its specific impact on type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and the underlying mechanisms, including the involvement of the serine/threonine kinase AKT, remain unclear. A T2DM animal model was induced using a high-fat diet and streptozotocin injection, and an insulin-resistant cell model was established via glucosamine treatment. Chronic treatment with BP for eight weeks ameliorated hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia and restored glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in a murine model of T2DM. Histologically, BP reduced hepatic steatosis and preserved hepatic glycogen reserves. At the hepatic level, BP treatment was accompanied by increased GSK3β Ser9 phosphorylation, reduced phosphorylation of the inflammatory mediators IκBα and NF-κB, decreased mRNA expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and reduced expression of the endoplasmic reticulum stress-related proteins GRP78 and IRE1α. Network pharmacology and pathway enrichment identified PI3K-AKT signaling as a pathway of interest, while molecular docking suggested a potential BP-AKT1 interaction. In insulin-resistant HepG2 cells, the AKT inhibitor MK-2206 attenuated several BP-associated effects. Taken together, these findings are consistent with an involvement of AKT signaling in the effects of BP on hepatic glycogen-related changes, inflammation, and endoplasmic reticulum stress in T2DM. These results provide a basis for further investigation of BP in T2DM and its associated hepatic metabolic dysfunction.
AI_Summary: Bergapten, a natural compound found in traditional Chinese medicinal herbs, shows promise in treating type 2 diabetes and related liver issues. In a recent study using diabetic mice and liver cells, long-term treatment with bergapten successfully lowered high blood sugar, restored insulin sensitivity, and reduced harmful fat accumulation in the liver. It also decreased liver inflammation and cellular stress. Researchers discovered that bergapten achieves these benefits primarily by interacting with a key protein pathway (called AKT) that helps cells store sugar properly and manage stress. Overall, these findings suggest that bergapten could be a valuable natural option for managing type 2 diabetes and protecting liver health.

Title: Hyperinsulinemia contributes to regulatory T-cell dysfunction and disease activity in multiple sclerosis.
Original_Abstract: We examined relationships among obesity, hyperinsulinemia, regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, and activity in multiple sclerosis (MS), and investigated insulin signaling as a candidate mechanism. We prospectively followed 131 patients with relapsing-remitting MS, stratified by body mass index, for at least 36 months. Clinical and MRI outcomes were assessed longitudinally, whereas metabolic parameters and Treg phenotype and function were evaluated at baseline. Mechanistic studies examined insulin receptor signaling in purified Tregs using insulin stimulation, pharmacological inhibition, insulin receptor silencing, and functional assays. In a separate, non-overlapping cohort, 28 obese hyperinsulinemic patients with relapsing-remitting MS underwent a 24-week metformin intervention with longitudinal metabolic and immunological assessments. Obese patients had higher fasting insulin, more relapses, disability progression, and MRI activity. Hyperinsulinemia correlated with reduced FoxP3 and IL-10, impaired Treg suppression, and increased IFN-γ and IL-17 in Treg-enriched cultures. Insulin stimulation altered AKT-mTOR signaling and Treg function; AKT inhibition or insulin receptor silencing reversed these effects. Obese-patient Tregs suppressed myelin-reactive responses less effectively. During metformin treatment, reductions in fasting insulin and AKT-mTOR signaling were accompanied by improvements in Treg phenotype and suppressive function and attenuation of myelin-specific inflammatory responses. These immunological changes correlated with insulin reductions, but the single-arm design and metformin's direct effects preclude causal attribution. These findings support an association between hyperinsulinemia, altered Treg function, and inflammatory disease activity in MS and identify insulin signaling as a candidate pathway for further mechanistic investigation.
AI_Summary: This study found that high insulin levels associated with obesity may worsen multiple sclerosis (MS) by weakening key protective immune cells. Normally, these specialized immune cells help keep the body's defense system from causing harm, but excess insulin disrupts them, leading to more frequent MS relapses and worse symptoms. When researchers treated obese MS patients with an insulin-lowering diabetes medication, these protective immune cells recovered and harmful inflammation decreased. Ultimately, the findings suggest that high insulin plays a role in driving MS flares and that lowering insulin levels could be a useful strategy to help manage the disease.

Title: Box H/ACA snoRNP regulates development and lipid metabolism in Drosophila melanogaster.
Original_Abstract: Lipid homeostasis is essential for organismal function, as its disruption drives various metabolic disorders. Using an unbiased genetic modifier screen in Drosophila, we identified GAR1, a core component of the box H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex, as a key regulator of systemic lipid storage. H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein dysfunction reduces lipid droplet size in the fat body cells and promotes ectopic fat accumulation in the salivary gland cells. Null mutants of Gar1, Nop60B, and Nop10 display severe developmental defects, including reduced body size and larval lethality, whereas NHP2 null mutants die at the embryonic stage, indicating that this complex is critical for normal development. RNA-seq analysis, followed by RT-PCR validation, revealed that Gar1 dysfunction perturbs the splicing of sgg, which encodes a key regulator of insulin signaling. Consistently, knockdown of Gar1 or Nop60B impaired PI3K/AKT signaling, as evidenced by reduced membrane localization of the tGPH, a GFP reporter for PIP3 in the salivary gland cells. Notably, overexpression of Akt suppressed the reduction in lipid storage in Gar1-silenced flies. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized link between the H/ACA small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex and metabolic processes, such as lipid storage and development, and support the role of this complex as a regulator that may be functionally linked to insulin signaling.
AI_Summary: Maintaining the right balance of fat is essential for an organism's health and survival. Studying fruit flies, researchers discovered that a specific protein called GAR1 plays a critical role in controlling how fat is stored and how the body grows. When GAR1 or its associated protein group malfunctions, flies fail to store fat correctly, accumulate unwanted fat in the wrong tissues, suffer severe growth defects, and die early. The study revealed that GAR1 works by supporting normal insulin signaling, a crucial process that manages energy and cell growth. Restoring this insulin pathway fixed the fat storage issues, uncovering an important new link between basic cellular machinery and overall metabolic health.

Title: Targeting Energy Metabolism and Tryptophan Pathways in Alzheimer's Disease for Developing Therapeutic Strategies.
Original_Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the primary cause of dementia worldwide and carries a high socioeconomic burden. However, despite the fact that such pathological features as amyloid-beta plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are considered hallmark traits of AD, therapeutic approaches targeting these pathological features have shown limited clinical efficacy to date. Recent scientific discoveries have drawn attention to the importance of metabolic processes preceding neurodegeneration. Reduced glucose utilization and impaired oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) are associated with bioenergetic deficits that may increase neuronal vulnerability to damage. In addition, neuroinflammation is associated with altered tryptophan metabolism through the kynurenine pathway and may favor the production of potentially neurotoxic metabolites. Despite these separate aspects of AD, the interaction between impaired bioenergetics and altered tryptophan metabolism in the brain has not been sufficiently studied. This gap complicates the development of multi-targeted treatment strategies. The purpose of this narrative review is to examine how gut dysbiosis, immune activation, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) impairment, redox imbalance, and tryptophan-kynurenine pathway dysregulation interact and may contribute to AD development and progression, including associated neuropsychiatric symptoms. We examine whether NAD⁺ depletion and rerouting of tryptophan metabolism may act as key nodes linking mitochondrial respiratory failure with the generation of neurotoxic kynurenine metabolites, excitotoxic glutamatergic signaling, loss of neurotrophic support, and synaptic dysfunction, and to analyze existing and emerging therapeutic strategies that target these interconnected pathways. In addition, this review highlights potentially promising interventions, such as NAD⁺ precursor supplementation, central nervous system insulin delivery, and modification of gut microbiome. Here we propose that the energy-tryptophan metabolic axis is a promising but underexplored area of AD research. Targeting these convergent bioenergetic and metabolomic pathways may support precision intervention strategies that could extend beyond conventional amyloid-centric paradigms to address broader neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric syndromes.
AI_Summary: Traditional Alzheimer’s treatments focus on clearing protein build-ups in the brain, but these have had limited success. Newer research suggests that the disease may actually be driven by early problems with how the brain creates and uses energy. When brain cells suffer from energy shortages, it triggers a chain reaction involving inflammation, unhealthy gut bacteria, and the production of toxic chemicals that damage brain cells. By targeting this link between energy loss, inflammation, and chemical imbalances, researchers hope to move beyond traditional methods. Promising new approaches include boosting vital energy molecules in cells, delivering insulin directly to the brain, and improving gut health to protect against brain damage and slow the disease down.

Title: Lifespan-Extending Downregulation of Insulin Signalling Reduces Germline Mutation Load.
Original_Abstract: Reduced insulin/IGF-1 signalling (IIS) robustly extends lifespan and enhances somatic stress resistance across taxa, yet its consequences for germline genome integrity remain unclear. Here we combine multigenerational mutation accumulation with whole-genome sequencing in Caenorhabditis elegans to test whether adulthood-only IIS downregulation can simultaneously promote somatic maintenance and limit germline mutational burden. We reduced IIS by adult-onset daf-2 RNAi in wild-type and heritable RNAi-deficient (hrde-1) backgrounds, allowing either spontaneous or UV-induced germline mutations to accumulate over multiple generations. In wild-type animals, reduced IIS lowered germline single-nucleotide mutation rates by up to ~50% and prevented the UV-induced elevation in mutation rate, without detectable costs to fecundity or lineage persistence. By contrast, in hrde-1 mutants the same intervention increased both point mutations and transposable-element-driven insertions under UV exposure, accelerating lineage extinction. Thus, the genome-protective effect of reduced IIS critically requires the germline nuclear Argonaute HRDE-1, which mediates small-RNA-guided epigenetic silencing. Functional annotation of germline variants revealed enrichment in pathways linked to development, cellular maintenance and conserved longevity regulators, including IIS and mTOR, and identified high-impact mutations in genes with human orthologs implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer. Our findings show that IIS can coordinate somatic and germline maintenance in concert, rather than in competition, through an HRDE-1-dependent epigenetic pathway. This work positions nutrient-sensing IIS as a central regulator of germline genome stability and suggests that IIS downregulation can reduce germline mutation load while extending lifespan, with broad implications for biogerontology and evolutionary biology.
AI_Summary: Scientists have long known that lowering insulin signaling helps animals live longer and resist stress, but its effect on the DNA passed down to future generations was previously unclear. By studying roundworms, researchers discovered that reducing insulin signaling in adults actually cuts DNA mutations in their offspring by up to 50% and protects their genetic code from radiation damage, all without reducing fertility. However, this genetic shield relies on a key protective protein; without it, lowering insulin actually increases DNA damage. Ultimately, these findings show that reducing insulin signaling does not force a trade-off between living a longer life and keeping offspring healthy—it coordinates the protection of both the parent's body and the genetic health of future generations at the same time.

Title: Enhanced stem cell-derived pancreatic β cell production through mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming improves islet cell therapy for diabetes.
Original_Abstract: The scarcity of functional transplantable pancreatic islets remains a central limitation for curative cell replacement therapies for diabetes. Although human pluripotent stem cells provide a theoretically unlimited source of β cells, intrinsic metabolic constraints that restrict efficient endocrine lineage commitment and functional maturation are poorly defined. We combined metabolic pathway interrogation with functional and in vivo analyses to examine how mitochondrial redox signaling influences endocrine specification during human pluripotent stem cell differentiation. Targeted modulation of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species-linked arachidonic acid and eicosanoid metabolism was used to assess its impact on β-cell differentiation, maturation, and therapeutic performance following transplantation. We identify a previously unrecognized mitochondrial reactive oxygen species-driven arachidonic acid/12-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid metabolic axis that functions as a metabolic checkpoint limiting endocrine lineage commitment. Disruption of this pathway markedly enhances the generation of stem cell-derived β cells and accelerates their functional maturation, resulting in improved glucose-responsive insulin secretion in vitro. Notably, β cells produced through this metabolic reprogramming strategy restore normoglycaemia more rapidly and robustly after transplantation into diabetic mice than cells generated using conventional differentiation protocols. These findings define a mechanistic link between mitochondrial redox signaling and eicosanoid metabolism in β-cell fate control and establish metabolic pathway engineering as a powerful strategy to improve the efficacy of stem cell-based islet replacement therapies for diabetes.
AI_Summary: Stem cell therapies offer a promising cure for diabetes by creating new insulin-producing cells, but getting stem cells to mature into fully functional cells has been a major challenge. Researchers discovered a specific metabolic pathway that acts like a brake, holding stem cells back from properly developing into these vital cells. By blocking this pathway, the team was able to speed up the maturation process and produce cells that secrete insulin much more effectively. When tested in diabetic mice, these newly engineered cells restored healthy blood sugar levels faster and more reliably than standard methods, offering a powerful new approach to improving stem-cell treatments for diabetes.

Title: Chemogenetics reveals a surprising role for GPR18 signaling in immunometabolic regulation of β cell activity.
Original_Abstract: Pancreatic islet macrophages are important immunometabolic regulators of β cell function, particularly in obesity-associated type 2 diabetes. Previous studies have established that pancreatic islet macrophages communicate with β cells through either the release of cytokines and growth factors, or direct cell-cell contact. In this issue of the JCI, Singh et al. used chemogenetics to identify a Gq/AMPK pathway that remodels sphingolipid metabolism. This pathway links macrophages to β cells through a CD36-dependent mechanism that reduces insulin secretion. Surprisingly, the orphan GPCR GPR18 was identified as the receptor that engages this pathway. These findings expand our understanding in macrophage-β cell communication and identify GPR18 as a potential therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes.
AI_Summary: Immune cells in the pancreas play a key role in controlling insulin-producing cells, which is particularly important in obesity-related type 2 diabetes. A new study discovered that a specific protein, called GPR18, acts as a switch inside these immune cells to trigger a pathway that reduces insulin secretion. By showing exactly how these immune cells communicate with insulin-producing cells to lower insulin levels, this research highlights GPR18 as a promising new target for developing future diabetes treatments.

Title: Sesamin Ameliorates Insulin Resistance in Association With Gut Microbiota Remodeling and ICA-AhR-GLP-1 Signaling in Diabetic Mice.
Original_Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is closely associated with insulin resistance and gut microbiota dysbiosis. Here, we identified a microbiota-associated indole-3-carboxaldehyde (ICA)-AhR-GLP-1 pathway that contributes to the glucose-lowering effect of sesamin (Ses), a major sesame lignan. In db/db mice, Ses improved hyperglycemia and insulin resistance, while remodeling the gut microbiota and enriching Ligilactobacillus. Fecal microbiota transplantation from Ses-treated donors partially transferred these metabolic benefits. Integrated bacterial isolation, Ses-based fermentation, fecal metabolomics, and clinical LC-MS/MS analysis identified ICA as a Ses-responsive microbiota-associated metabolite. Serum ICA levels were reduced in newly diagnosed patients with T2DM and negatively correlated with FBG, HbA1c, and HOMA-IR. Oral ICA reproduced key metabolic effects of Ses and enhanced intestinal Gcg expression and GLP-1 production. Mechanistically, ICA bound to AhR, promoted AhR nuclear translocation, increased AhR occupancy at the XRE-containing region of the Gcg promoter, and stimulated GLP-1 secretion in STC-1 cells and intestinal organoids. AhR inhibition reduced Ses-induced GLP-1 production and partially attenuated its metabolic effects, whereas acute GLP-1R blockade blunted Ses- and ICA-induced improvements in glucose tolerance and early insulin secretion. Together, these findings support a model in which Ses improves glucose homeostasis in association with gut microbiota remodeling and engagement of an ICA-AhR-GLP-1 pathway.
AI_Summary: A natural compound found in sesame seeds, called sesamin, helps manage type 2 diabetes by improving gut health. Researchers discovered that sesamin alters gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce a beneficial substance called ICA, which is typically low in people with diabetes. This substance then triggers the body to release a key hormone that regulates blood sugar and improves insulin response. Overall, sesamin helps control blood sugar levels by reshaping the gut environment to naturally boost this sugar-regulating hormone.

Title: Maternal BMI modulates cord plasma NT-proBNP in gestational diabetes linking cardiac stress to insulin-cortisol crosstalk.
Original_Abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is an increasingly prevalent pregnancy disorder associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, including an increased risk of early-onset cardiovascular disease in infants. GDM is associated with cardiac structural and functional changes as early as in utero. However, pathways linking maternal metabolic status to fetal cardiac stress remain poorly defined. We investigated N-teminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) in umbilical cord plasma (UCP) as a candidate biomarker of fetal cardiac stress, together with additional cardiac, endocrine and endothelial biomarkers to identify novel links between fetal cardiac health and maternal and fetal metabolic, inflammatory and hormonal characteristics. UCP from 82 term pregnancies (57 controls, 25 GDM) was analyzed for NT-proBNP and complementary cardiac, endocrine, and endothelial markers. Associations with maternal metabolic parameters, neonatal outcomes, and other UCP parameters were assessed using correlation, regression, and mediation analyses, adjusted for gestational age and neonatal sex. NT-proBNP levels were elevated in the cord plasma of GDM pregnancies, specifically in the presence of increased maternal pre-pregnancy BMI. Across the cohort, NT-proBNP was further associated with maternal BMI at delivery, fasting glucose levels, placental weight, and neonatal C-peptide, while inversely associated with cord plasma cortisol. Mediation analyses identified a significant indirect association involving neonatal C-peptide and suggested a potential mediating role of NT-proBNP in the association between maternal pre-pregnancy BMI and cord plasma cortisol. These findings suggest that NT-proBNP may reflect fetal cardiac load in GDM and is associated with maternal metabolic status and fetal insulin secretion. The inverse association between NT-proBNP and cortisol raises the possibility of an interplay between natriuretic peptide signaling and glucocorticoid regulation, pointing towards a potential cardiac-endocrine adaptation to intrauterine metabolic stress. While these observations deserve further investigation, they provide new insights into cardiovascular programming.
AI_Summary: Gestational diabetes can increase the risk of heart problems in babies, but researchers are still trying to understand how a mother's health affects her unborn child's heart. A recent study analyzed umbilical cord blood to measure a specific protein that acts as an indicator of heart stress. Researchers found that babies born to mothers with gestational diabetes—especially those whose mothers were overweight before pregnancy—had significantly higher levels of this stress protein. These elevated levels were closely tied to higher maternal blood sugar, increased fetal insulin production, and altered stress hormone levels in the baby. Overall, these findings suggest that a mother's weight and diabetes can place measurable stress on her developing baby's heart, offering important new clues about how early life in the womb shapes long-term heart health.

Title: Hormonal Influence on Breast Cancer Progression.
Original_Abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide. Beyond classical estrogen receptor-alpha (ERα) and progesterone receptor (PR) signaling, tumor progression, invasion, and treatment resistance are increasingly linked to an interconnected endocrine-metabolic network involving insulin, insulin-like growth factors (IGF-1/IGF-2), thyroid hormones (T3/T4), catecholamines, adrenal steroids, prolactin, and growth hormone within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Following systematic searches of PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through September 2025, 141 primary and translational studies were evaluated in this narrative review. Evidence was categorized according to experimental context: in vitro models, animal xenografts and patient-derived xenografts, and human clinical or epidemiological studies. Endocrine-metabolic resistance was characterized as a mechanism through which tumor cells may circumvent ER/HER2-targeted therapies via hyperinsulinemia-associated insulin receptor/IGF-1R signaling, aerobic glycolysis, thyroid hormone-mediated receptor phosphorylation, and sympathetic/adrenergic remodeling of the TME. Hypoxia was associated with radioresistance, whereas reoxygenation enhanced radiosensitivity; trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1) was recognized as having clinically relevant toxicities, including thrombocytopenia and hepatotoxicity; non-canonical progesterone signaling was considered in PR-negative and triple-negative breast cancer phenotypes; and PR downregulation was associated with anti-estrogen treatment. Resistance to single-receptor-targeted therapies may be promoted by redundant metabolic and neuroendocrine signaling. Improved therapeutic outcomes may require biomarker-guided combination strategies incorporating selective estrogen receptor degraders, CDK4/6, AKT, and PI3Kα inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates, and metabolic interventions, including metformin and glycemic control.
AI_Summary: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of death among women partly because tumors often find ways to resist standard treatments. Rather than relying on just one pathway to grow, cancer cells can adapt by using back-up signals from a complex network of hormones and body processes—including insulin, thyroid, and stress hormones. Because targeting a single pathway allows the tumor to bypass treatment using these back-up routes, single-drug therapies often fail over time. To improve outcomes, future treatments will likely require personalized combination strategies that pair targeted cancer drugs with metabolic treatments, such as blood sugar management, to block the tumor from adapting and spreading.

Title: Research Progress of Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 in Major Neurodegenerative Diseases.
Original_Abstract: Major neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) represent a large category of disorders characterized by the progressive loss of structure, function, or eventual death of neuronal cells in the brain and spinal cord. Current conventional therapeutic strategies for NDDs primarily focus on symptomatic relief. In contrast, IGF-1 is a pleiotropic protein with neurotrophic, synaptogenic, and anti-apoptotic properties, and its neuroprotective potential has been demonstrated in various preclinical models of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and other NDDs. However, the clinical efficacy of IGF-1-based interventions-whether for symptomatic relief or disease modification-has not been established in humans. Research on IGF-1 as a therapeutic target for NDDs remains predominantly preclinical, and its translation into effective clinical treatments requires further validation. This narrative review summarizes the mechanisms of action and therapeutic advances of IGF-1 in the progression of NDDs, encompassing the following four aspects: (1) Strategies based on signaling pathway regulation that target key pathways such as IGF-1/PI3K/Akt to reduce neuronal loss, promote synaptogenesis and structural remodeling, correct anomalous tau hyperphosphorylation, and improve amyloid-β (Aβ) clearance impairment. (2) Strategies based on restoring central sensitivity that focus on ameliorating cerebral insulin/IGF-1 resistance and utilizing agents to indirectly restore the neuroprotective function of IGF-1, thereby delaying cognitive decline. (3) Strategies based on delivery systems: in animal models, these employ viral vectors or nanomaterials to achieve targeted brain delivery of IGF-1, effectively promoting the survival of dopaminergic and motor neurons. (4) Future research directions that further elucidate the dynamic evolution of IGF-1 signaling across different disease stages and the development of stage-specific regulatory strategies. This review discusses approaches to restoring central IGF-1 signaling, ameliorating cerebral insulin resistance, and improving brain-targeted delivery, while emphasizing that their therapeutic relevance remains predominantly preclinical and requires validation in human studies.
AI_Summary: Current treatments for brain diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's only manage symptoms, but a natural protein called IGF-1 may help protect and repair damaged brain cells. Laboratory and animal studies show that IGF-1 can keep brain cells alive, strengthen their connections, and help clear out toxic proteins linked to memory loss. Researchers are currently exploring advanced delivery methods—such as microscopic particles—to get the protein directly into the brain and help the brain respond to it more effectively. While IGF-1 shows great promise in early scientific research, more human trials are needed to prove whether it can become a safe and effective treatment.

Title: Theoretical Considerations Regarding the Role of Hyperinsulinemia and Insulin/IGF Signaling in Cancer Metabolic Reprogramming: Potential Mechanisms and Therapeutic Vulnerabilities.
Original_Abstract: Hyperinsulinemia is increasingly recognized as a systemic factor that can promote tumor progression by amplifying insulin receptor and insulin-like growth factor (IGF) signaling, reshaping cancer-cell metabolism, and influencing the tumor microenvironment. Commonly associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, persistent hyperinsulinemia can enhance insulin/IGF receptor signaling and downstream PI3K-AKT-mTOR and RAS-MAPK pathways. These pathways interact with stress-response networks, including NRF2-dependent redox control and AMPK-autophagy signaling, thereby supporting metabolic plasticity under nutrient and microenvironmental stress. Hyperinsulinemia-associated signaling may increase glucose utilization, pentose phosphate pathway activity, glutaminolysis, de novo lipogenesis, and antioxidant capacity, collectively promoting anabolic growth, survival, and treatment adaptation. Metabolic remodeling extends beyond aerobic glycolysis and involves context-dependent alterations in mitochondrial function, oxidative metabolism, lactate production, and metabolic crosstalk among cancer, stromal, and immune cells. Consequently, hyperinsulinemia-associated signaling may contribute to lactate-rich, immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments, tumor progression, and heterogeneous therapeutic responses across cancer types. This review integrates experimental, epidemiological, and translational evidence linking persistent hyperinsulinemia and insulin/IGF signaling with cancer metabolic reprogramming. It critically examines strategies to reduce systemic insulin exposure, inhibit insulin/IGF signaling, or co-target tumor-specific metabolic dependencies, including the metabolic consequences of PI3K-pathway inhibition. By advancing a hyperinsulinemia-centered framework, this review identifies mechanistic gaps and translational priorities for more precise metabolic interventions in cancer.
AI_Summary: High levels of insulin in the blood, commonly caused by conditions like obesity and type 2 diabetes, can encourage cancer cells to grow and spread. Excess insulin alters the way cancer cells process energy, allowing them to consume nutrients more quickly, withstand stress, and adapt to resist medical treatments. It also changes the environment surrounding the tumor, weakening the immune system's ability to fight off the disease. Because of this strong link, researchers believe that finding ways to lower insulin levels or block insulin signals in the body could lead to smarter, more effective cancer therapies.

Title: Hen Egg-Derived Bioactive Proteins and Peptides at the Gut Interface: From Molecular Characterization and Digestion to Microbiome Interactions and Prospective Precision Nutrition.
Original_Abstract: Hen eggs (Gallus gallus domesticus) contain bioactive proteins, peptides and lipids, but compound characterization, mechanistic cell and animal studies, and human consumption trials have developed largely in isolation. This narrative review, supported by a documented literature search, follows one pathway: egg composition, molecular characterization, processing and digestion, bioaccessibility, intestinal and microbial interaction, host signaling, and a prospective precision-nutrition outlook. Findings are classified into translational evidence categories (a heuristic classification of experimental systems, not a ranking of study quality) and summarized in a multidimensional evidence matrix. Egg white and yolk proteins, including ovotransferrin, ovomucin and lysozyme, yield characterized peptides, notably the ovotransferrin tripeptides IRW (Ile-Arg-Trp), IQW (Ile-Gln-Trp) and LKP (Leu-Lys-Pro), and ovomucin hydrolysates, whose activities in cell and animal models are compound-specific: LKP, for example, did not reproduce the effect of IRW on insulin resistance in muscle cells. In humans, one small ileostomy study (n = 5) reports higher ileal protein digestibility for cooked than raw egg, short-term trials show that whole-egg intake raises plasma choline, and an antibiotic-suppression study shows that trimethylamine-N-oxide formation after eggs plus phosphatidylcholine depends on gut microbiota. No study identified shows that IRW, IQW or LKP are generated, survive digestion or reach the circulation after ordinary egg consumption, and only six human studies address egg intake and the gut microbiome. Dose-response, delivery-system and safety data are largely missing, and precision nutrition for egg bioactives remains a research framework. Priorities are human pharmacokinetic confirmation, longer trials with shotgun metagenomics and functional readouts, and independent safety testing.
AI_Summary: Although hen eggs contain many beneficial proteins and fats, scientists are still trying to understand how these nutrients actually work inside the human body. Laboratory and animal studies show that specific egg protein fragments offer potential health benefits, such as helping cells better respond to insulin. However, there is currently no proof that these beneficial compounds survive human digestion or reach the bloodstream when we eat normal eggs. While small human studies reveal that cooked eggs are easier to digest than raw ones and that gut bacteria help process egg nutrients, overall human research remains very limited. Moving forward, longer human trials are needed to confirm how the body absorbs these egg compounds, how they interact with gut health, and how safe they are at different doses.

Title: Structural Characterization and Hypoglycemic Mechanism of Pumpkin Seed Polysaccharides.
Original_Abstract: This study investigated three pumpkin seed polysaccharide fractions (PSP-1-1, PSP-1-2, and PSP-1-3) with molecular weights of 29,797 Da, 11,209 Da, and 4346 Da, respectively, all containing both α- and β-glycosidic linkages. Structural analysis revealed arabinose, galactose, and glucose as predominant residues in PSP-1-1, while PSP-1-2 and PSP-1-3 additionally contained xylose, with all fractions sharing common structural units. All three fractions were associated with dose-dependent increases in GLP-1 secretion from L cells and with upregulation of genes in the sweet taste receptor pathway. The pooled fraction PSP-1s showed higher gene expression than individual fractions and was therefore selected for in vivo studies. In diabetic mice, PSP-1s intervention alleviated weight loss, reduced hyperphagia and polydipsia, lowered blood glucose, improved glucose tolerance and dyslipidemia, and decreased GSP, insulin, and HOMA-IR while increasing QUICKI. Qualitative histological observations suggested less pronounced pancreatic islet abnormalities following PSP-1s intervention. PSP-1s increased serum GLP-1 concentrations and colonic SCFA concentrations and altered gut microbiota composition. Collectively, the hypoglycemic effects of PSP-1s were accompanied by changes in serum GLP-1, colonic SCFAs, gut microbiota composition, and hypothalamic GLP-1R and appetite-related gene expression. Together with the cellular findings, these observations suggest potential mechanisms involving sweet taste receptor-related signaling and microbiota-associated GLP-1 regulation. However, pathway activation and the causal contribution of gut-brain signaling remain to be established. These findings support further investigation of PSP-1s as a functional food ingredient with potential glucose-regulating activity.
AI_Summary: Researchers studied natural sugar compounds found in pumpkin seeds to see if they could help manage diabetes. In laboratory tests, these compounds triggered cells to release a key hormone that helps lower blood sugar and control appetite. When given to diabetic mice, the pumpkin seed extract successfully lowered blood sugar, improved insulin function, protected the pancreas, and reduced excessive hunger and thirst. It also promoted better gut health by improving the balance of beneficial gut bacteria. Overall, these findings suggest that pumpkin seed extracts could be a promising natural food ingredient to help regulate blood sugar and support diabetes management.

Title: ELOVL6 in the C16/C18 Ratio Control: An Emerging Regulator of Lipid and Glucose Metabolism.
Original_Abstract: Background/Objectives: Elongation of very long chain fatty acids protein 6 (ELOVL6) is a key enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of palmitoyl-CoA (C16:0-CoA) to stearoyl-CoA (C18:0-CoA). Its product C18:0-CoA is further desaturated by stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) to generate C18:1n-9-CoA. In this review, C18:0/C16:0 refers to the molar ratio of C18:0 to C16:0 within a specified lipid pool, such as acyl coenzyme A (acyl-CoA), total fatty acids, or phospholipids. It serves as a surrogate marker for ELOVL6 elongation flux under specific conditions. C18:1n-9/C18:0 refers to the oleic acid to stearic acid molar ratio. It serves as a surrogate marker for SCD1-related flux. C16:0/C18:1n-9 refers to the palmitic acid to oleic acid molar ratio. It is a composite readout influenced by both ELOVL6 and SCD1-related reactions. The "C16/C18 ratio" is used only as an umbrella term for C16/C18-related ratios. This review aims to explore how ELOVL6 modulates the balance of the C16/C18 ratio through molecular mechanisms. It also examines how this regulation contributes to glucose and lipid metabolism and to tissue-specific functions, and evaluates the potential of ELOVL6 as a therapeutic target for metabolic diseases. Methods: A structured literature search was conducted on recent advances regarding the enzymatic properties, transcriptional regulation, and animal model phenotypes of ELOVL6. A comprehensive synthesis was performed from molecular mechanisms to clinical translation. Results: In the liver, ELOVL6 mainly influences the direction of fatty acid storage and ceramide signaling. In adipose tissue, it influences insulin signal transduction by remodeling membrane phospholipid composition. In pancreatic β-cells, it affects insulin secretory function by contributing to the C16/C18 ratio. When the C16/C18 ratio becomes imbalanced, cells progress toward insulin resistance (IR), inflammation, and hepatic steatosis. Conclusions: Restoring the balance of the C16/C18 ratio is a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic diseases. However, targeting ELOVL6 faces challenges such as structural biology bottlenecks and tissue-specific side effects. Future research should focus on the fine regulation of ELOVL6, combined with dietary interventions, to advance the translation of ELOVL6 from basic research to clinical intervention for metabolic diseases.
AI_Summary: ELOVL6 is an enzyme that helps maintain a healthy balance of different types of fats in the body by converting shorter fat molecules into longer ones. This balance is crucial for keeping organs like the liver, fat tissue, and pancreas functioning properly. When this fat ratio gets out of balance, it can trigger metabolic problems such as chronic inflammation, fatty liver disease, and insulin resistance, which can lead to diabetes. Restoring this healthy fat balance by targeting ELOVL6 shows strong potential for treating metabolic diseases; however, creating safe drugs remains challenging due to possible tissue-specific side effects. Ultimately, combining therapies that adjust ELOVL6 activity with customized dietary changes may offer the safest path toward treating metabolic disorders.

Title: Xuanfei Baidu Decoction and Its Active Component Glycyrrhizic Acid Ameliorate Insulin Resistance in Type 2 Diabetes via JNK/JAK/STAT Axis Inhibition.
Original_Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is driven by insulin resistance and chronic inflammation, yet current single-target therapies inadequately address these interconnected pathologies. Xuanfei Baidu decoction (XFBD), originally developed for COVID-19, is known to inhibit JNK and JAK/STAT pathways and may offer a multi-target strategy. A high sugar diet (HSD) induced Drosophila T2DM model was treated with XFBD or its active component glycyrrhizic acid (GA). Phenotypic assays, metabolomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, qPCR, transgenic reporter flies, network pharmacology, and computational docking/dynamics simulations were performed. XFBD dose-dependently alleviated HSD-induced developmental delay, hyperglycemia, insulin resistance (restored dilp2/3/5, InR, 4EBP expression and AKT phosphorylation), glycolipid disorders, and oxidative stress. Metabolomics identified 79 reversed metabolites enriched in T2DM-relevant pathways (D-amino acid, BCAA, TCA cycle). XFBD suppressed aberrant JNK and JAK/STAT activation, independent of gut microbiota modulation. GA recapitulated these effects in vivo. XFBD and GA ameliorate insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation via JNK/JAK-STAT axis inhibition, providing a preclinical rationale for their therapeutic application in T2DM and related metabolic syndrome outcomes.
AI_Summary: Type 2 diabetes is a complex condition driven by both poor insulin response and chronic inflammation, making it difficult to treat with medications that focus on a single target. A recent study found that a traditional herbal formula (Xuanfei Baidu decoction) and its key active component (glycyrrhizic acid) effectively treated diabetes in fruit flies fed a high-sugar diet. The treatment successfully lowered high blood sugar, restored normal insulin function, improved fat and sugar processing, and reduced cellular stress. It accomplished this by turning down specific inflammatory signals in the body, offering a promising multi-target approach for treating type 2 diabetes and related metabolic disorders.

Title: Beyond conventional neurodiagnostic: quantum-enabled mapping of AGE-RAGE dynamics in type 3 diabetes.
Original_Abstract: Type 3 Diabetes (T3D) is a conceptual framework used to describe the association between cerebral insulin resistance, metabolic dysfunction and neurodegenerative processes, particularly those associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD). The advanced glycation end products (AGEs)-receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) axis has been implicated in oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling and neuronal dysfunction. However, conventional biochemical approaches often provide endpoint measurements and may not fully resolve the spatial and temporal dynamics of these processes. Advances in quantum sensing and nanotechnology offer potential tools for detecting selected physicochemical signals in biological systems, although their demonstrated capabilities vary substantially across platforms. This review examines the biological relevance of the AGE-RAGE axis in neurodegeneration and discusses the principles and types of quantum sensing technologies, including nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond and quantum dots, alongside other nanomaterial-based sensing approaches. Particular attention is given to probe functionalization, bioconjugation, signal transduction and experimental platforms that could support future investigations of AGE-RAGE-associated processes. Importantly, direct, real-time quantum sensing of AGE-RAGE interactions in living neuronal systems remain to be experimentally established. Accordingly, proposed applications involving receptor activation, downstream signaling, brain organoids, brain-on-chip systems and in vivo imaging are considered in terms of their potential, limitations and validation requirements. Challenges relating to target specificity, biological interference, biocompatibility, spatial and temporal resolution and translational feasibility are also discussed. This review outlines a prospective framework for investigating AGE-RAGE-associated signaling dynamics while distinguishing established sensing capabilities from applications that require further experimental validation.

Title: Knockdown of lncBNIP3 promotes proliferation and milk fat synthesis and alters cellular metabolism in bovine mammary epithelial cells.
Original_Abstract: Milk fat, an essential nutrient in the human diet, is primarily synthesized by bovine mammary epithelial cells (BMECs). Accumulating evidence indicates that long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate BMEC proliferation and milk fat synthesis. To investigate the role of lncBNIP3, we knocked down its expression in BMECs using siRNA and assessed the expression of proliferation-related genes by RT-qPCR and western blotting. The mRNA levels of PCNA, CCNB1, CCND1, CDK1, and CDK2 were significantly upregulated, and the protein levels of PCNA and CCNB1 were also markedly increased. EdU incorporation and flow cytometry assays demonstrated that lncBNIP3 knockdown promoted BMEC proliferation. Transcriptome sequencing following lncBNIP3 knockdown revealed that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were enriched in pathways related to the cell cycle and DNA replication. In BMECs induced to synthesize milk fat, lncBNIP3 knockdown significantly increased the mRNA levels of milk fat synthesis-related genes, such as FABP4, CEBPa, and PPARg, and elevated the protein levels of FABP4 and PPARg. Oil Red O staining and triglyceride quantification showed that lncBNIP3 downregulation promoted lipid droplet accumulation in BMECs. Transcriptomic analysis further indicated that DEGs upon lncBNIP3 knockdown were enriched in the mTOR and insulin signaling pathways. Finally, untargeted metabolomics analysis after lncBNIP3 knockdown identified 187 differential metabolites, including carboxylic acids and derivatives, glycerophospholipids, and fatty acyls. Among these, the levels of multiple glycerophospholipid species were significantly lower. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of differential metabolites highlighted pathways such as ABC transporters, vitamin digestion and absorption, regulation of lipolysis in adipocytes, and glycerophospholipid metabolism, which are involved in protein, vitamin, and lipid metabolism. In summary, lncBNIP3 knockdown promotes BMEC proliferation and milk fat synthesis. The underlying mechanisms may involve the cell cycle and DNA replication pathways in mediating proliferation, and the mTOR and insulin signaling pathways in regulating milk fat synthesis. Furthermore, lncBNIP3 knockdown modulates protein, vitamin, and lipid metabolism in BMECs.

Title: Metabolic syndrome and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic links and precision prevention (Review).
Original_Abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD), however, the majority of previous studies regard MetS as an isolated risk factor and focus on single pathways, lacking systematic understanding of combined effects among multiple metabolic components. The present review systematically summarizes the multifaceted mechanisms by which MetS promotes AD pathology, including insulin resistance and cerebral energy dysregulation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation and glial cell activation, vascular dysfunction and dysregulation of the renin‑angiotensin system, as well as the central convergent signaling pathway involving glycogen synthase kinase‑3β. The present review further highlights emerging regulatory mechanisms involving the gut‑brain axis, epigenetic reprogramming, sex differences and hormonal effects and senescent microenvironment. By emphasizing the peripheral‑central crosstalk and interactive amplification of MetS components, the present review aimed to position AD as a central manifestation of systemic metabolic disorders in the brain and propose a multi‑domain precision strategy integrating lifestyle intervention, metabolic drug repurposing, gut microbiota regulation, anti‑aging therapy and biomarker‑guided subtype classification for intervention against MetS‑associated AD.

Title: IRS-1 phase separation bridges IGF-1R signaling and the MITF/TYR axis to control melanogenesis.
Original_Abstract: Melanogenesis is well known to be activated by the α-MSH/MITF signaling pathway. Recent studies have further revealed that the IGF-1/IGF-1R metabolic signaling axis can also induce melanin synthesis. Here, we demonstrate that IRS-1, a key downstream adaptor of both IGF-1R and the insulin receptor (IR), acts as a bridge by connecting the upstream IGF-1R signaling with the downstream MITF/TYR axis to promote melanogenesis. Importantly, this function of IRS-1 may be tissue-specific, as insulin alone fails to stimulate melanogenesis. Deletion of the self-interaction region (SAR) abolishes the phase separation of IRS-1, thereby preventing the activation of melanogenesis. Taken together, our findings reveal a novel function of IRS-1 phase separation in melanogenesis. This work not only sheds light on understanding the regulatory mechanism of melanin homeostasis but also provides a potential strategy for cosmetics companies to develop more effective whitening products.

Title: Single-cell transcriptomic landscape delineates pathogenic NK cell subpopulations and key mediators in systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
Original_Abstract: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) carries high ICU morbidity, sepsis lacks standardized therapies, and stage-variable natural killer (NK) cell function in SIRS remains poorly defined due to insufficient single-cell evidence. Herein, we analyzed public LPS-induced SIRS peripheral blood single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data (GSE212092) via multiple bioinformatic algorithms to dissect NK heterogeneity, followed by in vitro functional verification using NK-92 cells with IGF1 stimulation or IGF1R knockdown. We identified distinct cell types and 6 distinct NK subpopulations (C0-C5). Pro-inflammatory C0 and proliferative C2 IGF1R⁺ expanded in early SIRS, whereas stemness-high C3-C5 accumulated during late immunosuppression. MHC-I and CCL5-CCR1 dominated NK-related intercellular crosstalk, and unique transcription regulatory modules existed across NK subpopulations. Functional assays verified IGF1/IGF1R signaling dose-dependently promotes NK inflammatory cytokine release, cytotoxic gene expression, cell viability and target cell killing. These findings delineate dynamic NK subpopulation remodeling during SIRS and validate IGF1/IGF1R as a potential key pathway governing NK effector function, providing a transcriptomic basis for identifying candidate biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets in SIRS.

Title: Sleep and circadian disruption as systemic drivers of breast cancer metastasis: A tri-pathway mechanistic model.
Original_Abstract: Sleep deficiency and circadian disruption are emerging modifiable risk factors in breast cancer. However, their specific role in driving metastasis remains incompletely defined. This review maps circadian disturbance to metastatic competence through three convergent systemic pathways. First is neuroendocrine disruption via melatonin suppression. Second is immunological dysregulation characterized by chronic inflammation and myeloid derived suppressor cell expansion. Third is metabolic reprogramming involving insulin resistance and altered adipokine signaling. These converging signals lower critical barriers at every step of metastasis. They promote epithelial mesenchymal transition and local invasion. They support circulating tumor cell survival. They enable pre metastatic niche formation. They also trigger reactivation of dormant micrometastases. We evaluate clinical biomarkers of circadian disruption including cortisol rhythms, urinary melatonin, and actigraphy. We link these sleep metrics to patient outcomes. We also discuss therapeutic opportunities such as melatonin supplementation, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, and personalized chrono chemotherapy. By establishing circadian health as an actionable axis in metastasis prevention, this review provides a framework for integrating chronobiology into breast cancer management and survivorship care.

Title: Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus L.) extract alleviates insulin resistance in gestational diabetes mellitus by modulating the AKT/LRRFIP1/GLUT4 pathway in skeletal muscle.
Original_Abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is characterized by progressive insulin resistance (IR), with skeletal muscle representing a primary site of this pathology. This study investigated the potential of anthocyanin-rich bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus L.) extract (VME) to ameliorate skeletal muscle IR in a high-fat diet (HFD) induced rat model of GDM. We integrated proteomics and bioinformatics approaches to elucidate the underlying mechanisms.UHPLC-MS/MS analysis identified cyanidin-3-O-galactoside (C3Gal) as the principal anthocyanin constituent of VME. Daily oral administration of VME (400 mg per kg bw) during pregnancy ameliorated hyperglycemia, IR, and dyslipidemia, and improved oral glucose tolerance in GDM rats. Proteomic analysis of gastrocnemius muscle identified VME associated differentially expressed proteins as candidate targets for further investigation. Gene set enrichment analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis implicated AKT signaling and highlighted Lrrfip1 as a hub gene correlated with HOMA-IR. Cross-species comparison with human type 2 diabetes skeletal muscle transcriptomes (GSE55650, GSE7014) supported target prioritization, with LRRFIP1 showing concordant regulation at both mRNA and protein levels. Molecular docking predicted binding of C3Gal to AKT and LRRFIP1, and a cellular thermal shift assay supported cellular target engagement of C3Gal with these proteins. C3Gal restored p-AKT and GLUT4 levels both in vivo and in palmitate-induced C2C12 myotubes. siRNA mediated knockdown of Lrrfip1 attenuated these effects, whereas pharmacological inhibition of AKT abolished them. Collectively, these findings support LRRFIP1 as a downstream mediator of AKT associated GLUT4 regulation. Together, our data propose LRRFIP1 as a candidate molecular target associated with skeletal muscle IR and support further investigation of VME as a potential dietary intervention for GDM associated IR.

Title: HbA1c and skeletal muscle health in type 2 diabetes: phenotype-specific associations across different analytical directions and mechanistic insights.
Original_Abstract: Sarcopenia is increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), but its association with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) remains unclear. This review synthesizes evidence from 30 clinical reports examining the relationship between HbA1c-derived glycemic exposure measures and skeletal muscle outcomes in adults with T2DM, with studies categorized by muscle phenotype and analytical direction. Risk of bias was assessed using design-specific JBI checklists (lower/moderate/higher concern:11/16/3), and conclusions emphasized adjusted estimates from lower or moderate-concern studies. Available evidence indicates that the association between HbA1c-derived glycemic exposure measures and skeletal muscle health differs substantially across phenotypes. Longitudinal studies provide more consistent temporal evidence linking HbA1c trajectories to changes in muscle mass, whereas some prospective studies suggest that baseline muscle characteristics may provide prognostic information regarding subsequent glycemic outcomes. Evidence for physical performance remains inconsistent, and associations with composite sarcopenia vary according to diagnostic frameworks and phenotype composition. Potential biological mechanisms involving impaired insulin signaling, advanced glycation end product accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, neuropathy, and microvascular impairment may represent biologically plausible and overlapping pathways contributing to these associations. However, direct human evidence supporting pathway-specific effects on individual muscle phenotypes remains limited. Current evidence supports a phenotype-specific interpretation of the HbA1c-skeletal muscle relationship but does not establish bidirectional causality. HbA1c should be interpreted as a marker of glycemic exposure rather than an indicator of overall skeletal muscle health, and satisfactory glycemic control does not exclude sarcopenia or impairment in individual muscle domains. Prospective studies with repeated glycemic assessments and multidimensional muscle evaluations are needed to clarify temporal relationships and clinical implications.

Title: Context-dependent pharmacological effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists in breast cancer from molecular mechanisms to clinical safety.
Original_Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have become cornerstone therapeutics for type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity, but their impact on breast cancer remains uncertain. Preclinical studies show context-dependent effects of GLP-1 RAs on breast-cancer cells. Direct evidence from breast-cancer models supports a pro-proliferative NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4)/reactive oxygen species (ROS) /VEGF pathway under supra-pharmacological exposure, whereas PI3K/Akt-mediated pro-survival signaling and cAMP/PKA/CREB-driven proliferation remain inferred from non-breast systems and require direct confirmation. Under obesity- and insulin-resistant conditions, indirect antitumor effects may occur through improved insulin sensitivity, altered adipokines, and remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials do not show a significant increase in breast-cancer risk (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.76-1.26), while some large observational cohorts report small risk differences that are susceptible to confounding and detection bias. Evidence for inter-agent differences is observational and limited by the absence of head-to-head randomized oncological comparisons. This narrative review synthesizes preclinical and clinical evidence across three dimensions, namely, molecular subtype, drug exposure, and host metabolic status, and distinguishes direct breast-cancer evidence from mechanistic extrapolation. We outline evidence-informed clinical considerations and research priorities rather than definitive recommendations.

Title: Neuroprotective effects of combination of ezetimibe and sericin against lead-induced neurotoxicity.
Original_Abstract: Chronic exposure to environmental pollutants, particularly heavy metals, has become a global health concern, reducing longevity. Among these, lead (Pb<sup>2+</sup>) is associated with neurobehavioral, neurodevelopmental, and neuropsychological impairments. Consequently, growing interest focuses on pharmacological and natural agents that restore neurotrophic signaling. Therefore, this study investigates neuroprotective effect of ezetimibe, an anti-hyperlipidemic agent, and sericin, a natural protein, in Pb<sup>2+</sup>-induced neurotoxicity in rats. Adult Wistar rats were divided into seven groups: control, lead acetate (PbAc<sub>2</sub>; 50 mg/kg), ezetimibe (10 and 20 mg/kg), sericin (200 and 400 mg/kg), and a combination of ezetimibe (10 mg/kg) and sericin (200 mg/kg) with PbAc<sub>2</sub>. PbAc<sub>2</sub> was administered for 55 days, while ezetimibe and sericin treatment was initiated on days 29-55. Behavioral assessments, including grip strength, open field test, and Morris water maze test, were performed. On day 56, animals were sacrificed, and hippocampal tissues were collected for neurochemical (GABA, GAD1, and dopamine) and mitochondrial complex 3 estimation, along with hippocampal histology. The qRT-PCR (Bax, Bcl2, caspase - 3, CREB, BDNF), western blot (IGF-1R, GLP-1R, PI3K, pAkt) were performed. The results demonstrated that PbAc<sub>2</sub> exposure induced behavioral deficits, neurotransmitter imbalance, disrupted mitochondrial-associated apoptotic pathway, and impaired neurotrophin signaling. Contrarily, ezetimibe and sericin, individually and in combination, significantly attenuated neurobehavioral impairments, restored neurochemical levels, improved mitochondrial complex III activity, suppressed apoptotic signaling, and preserved hippocampal histoarchitecture and enhanced synaptic plasticity through involvement of IGF-1R/GLP-1R signaling pathway. These findings suggest that ezetimibe and sericin, in combination, represent promising therapeutic candidates for mitigating PbAc<sub>2</sub>-induced neurotoxicity.

Title: Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analysis reveals molecular response characteristics to acute hypoxia stress in Culter alburnus.
Original_Abstract: Topmouth culter (Culter alburnus) is an economically important freshwater fish, yet the temporal responses of its liver to hypoxia stress remain poorly understood. This study investigated the changes in liver histological structure and antioxidant enzyme activities after different durations of hypoxia stress (L2H, L4H, L6H, L12H, and L24H). The results showed that the pathological damage gradually progressed from mild hepatic sinusoidal dilation to hepatocyte vacuolation. A significant decline in the antioxidant parameters (T-AOC, T-SOD, and CAT) was observed in the 6H group, which was followed by a slow rise. Furthermore, we performed a comparative analysis of the transcriptomes and metabolomes of the L6H, L24H, and control groups (LC). RNA-Seq analysis identified 2178 and 393 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the L6H-vs-LC and L24H-vs-LC groups, respectively. These DEGs were predominantly enriched in several pathways, including the HIF-1 signaling pathway, PPAR signaling pathway, and insulin signaling pathway. These findings suggested that hypoxia stress triggered a metabolic shift in C. alburnus through the enhanced efficiency of glycolytic energy supply. Metabolomic results revealed that 296 and 408 differential metabolites (DAMs) were identified in the L6H-vs-LC and L24H-vs-LC comparisons, respectively. These DAMs were mainly enriched in pathways associated with lipid remodeling, energy metabolism, and oxidative stress. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analysis revealed that the HIF-1 signaling pathway coordinately regulated gluconeogenesis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and glycerophospholipid metabolism. It cooperated with mTOR-mediated pathways and enhanced oxidative stress defense through FoxO family genes, thereby forming a multilayered metabolic adaptation network.

Title: ISX-9 marks the spot for better beta cell differentiation.
Original_Abstract: Stem cell-derived islets offer a promising approach to restoring endogenous insulin secretion in type 1 diabetes (T1D). In this issue of Developmental Cell, Zhao, Liang et al. show that ISX-9 expands PDX1+/NKX6-1+ pancreatic progenitors and improves beta-like cell yield and function, while revealing how extracellular matrix signaling regulates progenitor identity.

Title: ROS-dependent phosphorylation of insulin receptor and insulin receptor substrate during pupal diapause development in the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera.
Original_Abstract: Insect diapause is a critical adaptive strategy characterized by developmental arrest and enhanced stress tolerance, orchestrated by intricate molecular networks. The insulin signaling pathway, which governs growth, metabolism, and stress responses, has been implicated in diapause regulation. However, the precise roles of insulin receptor (InR) and insulin receptor substrate (IRS) in modulating pupal diapause remain incompletely understood, particularly in the economically important pest Helicoverpa armigera. Here, we show that InR and IRS are associated with pupal diapause development through redox-sensitive phosphorylation cascades. Temporal profiling revealed a marked upregulation of phosphorylated InR (p-InR) and IRS (p-IRS) in diapause-destined pupal brains, concomitant with elevated phosphorylation of Akt (p-Akt) and ERK (p-ERK). Functional validation in Helicoverpa zea (HzAm1) cells, via overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi), showed that IRS positively regulates Akt and ERK signaling. Further mechanistic studies indicated that reactive oxygen species (ROS) act upstream of the phosphorylation of InR, IRS, Akt, and ERK in vitro and in vivo; these effects were reversible upon ROS scavenging. Further investigations revealed that increased p-ERK was associated with global protein ubiquitination, suggesting this kinase as a key regulator of proteasomal degradation in diapause development. Our findings delineate a ROS-InR-IRS-Akt/ERK signaling framework associated with diapause development and proteostatic regulation in H. armigera, thereby advancing our understanding of insect diapause biology and providing candidate molecular targets for future pest-management interventions.

Title: Immunosenescence in Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome: A Unifying Mechanistic Framework.
Original_Abstract: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome is driven by a vicious cycle of metabolic dysregulation and chronic low-grade inflammation. Obesity catalyzes this process, causing apoptosis-resistant senescence-associated T (SA-T) cells to massively accumulate in visceral adipose tissue (VAT). These "rogue commanders" acquire a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), continuously producing osteopontin along with other proinflammatory cytokines and altering adipokine balance. Even after substantial weight loss, they survive, forming an immunological "risk memory" that sustains systemic inflammation and fibrotic tissue remodeling. Recent megatrials of incretin-based therapies (e.g., SELECT, STEP-HFpEF, FLOW, STRIDE, SOUL, and SURPASS-CVOT) demonstrate profound cardiorenal protection emerging independently of absolute weight reduction. Here, we propose a unifying mechanistic framework wherein these agents act as disease-modifying therapies by inducing an "immune and metabolic reset." By improving systemic insulin sensitivity, they eliminate the excessive growth stimulus on immune cells, thereby "quieting" the overdriven phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Akt/mammalian target of rapamycin pathway. Furthermore, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor activation exerts direct negative costimulatory effects on T cells, suppressing their activation. This metabolic quiescence reactivates autophagy, detoxifies SA-T cells, and halts SASP production, disrupting the vicious cycle of systemic inflammation. Reconceptualizing incretin therapies not merely as weight-loss drugs but as agents that erase immunological risk memory through optimized nutrient signaling provides a crucial paradigm shift in managing CKM syndrome.

Title: METTL3-IGF2BP1-dependent m6A methylation of LFNG drives oral squamous cell carcinoma progression.
