Original_Abstract: This study investigates the roles of methyltransferase-like protein 3 (METTL3) and insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 1 (IGF2BP1) within the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) regulatory axis in the progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), elucidating the underlying molecular mechanisms. We found that both METTL3 and IGF2BP1 are co-overexpressed in OSCC and synergistically enhance the proliferation, migration, and invasion capabilities of malignant tumors, while inhibiting apoptosis, as demonstrated in both in vitro and xenograft models. Transcriptomic analysis, combined with m6A immunoprecipitation experiments, confirmed that LFNG is a direct downstream effector subject to METTL3-mediated m6A methylation modification and is stabilized by IGF2BP1. Both loss-of-function and rescue experiments demonstrated that LFNG mediates all oncogenic phenotypes induced by the METTL3-IGF2BP1 axis; specifically, silencing either METTL3 or IGF2BP1 and subsequently overexpressing LFNG fully restores the malignant behavior and growth capabilities of the tumors. Mechanistically, the METTL3-IGF2BP1-dependent m6A modification stabilizes LFNG mRNA, thereby activating the Notch signaling pathway to accelerate OSCC progression. This study reveals that the METTL3-IGF2BP1-m6A-LFNG axis drives OSCC progression through transcriptomic epigenetic regulation. Targeting this regulatory pathway represents a promising strategy for the treatment of OSCC.

Title: Naofucong mitigates amyloid-β deposition and cognitive deficits by enhancing insulin-degrading enzyme expression and inhibiting BACE through MAPK pathway inhibition.
Original_Abstract: Amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation is a key pathological event in cognitive disorders. While the traditional Chinese medicine Naofucong has shown neuroprotective potential, its precise effects on Aβ metabolism remain unclear. This study investigated whether Naofucong modulates Aβ pathology by regulating key enzymes involved in its production and degradation. We employed Aβ-overexpressing 293-APP-BACE cells and treated them with Naofucong-containing serum. To further investigate the involvement of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway, the MAPK pathway inhibitor Trans-Zeatin (TZ) was used as a mechanistic reference tool to explore the involvement of MAPK signaling. This pharmacological inhibition approach was used to support the involvement of MAPK signaling in mediating the effects of Naofucong. Expression levels of insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE), amyloid precursor protein (APP), β-site APP cleaving enzyme (BACE), and Aβ were measured. In addition, the activation status of MAPK signaling (ERK, JNK, p38) was assessed. Naofucong-containing serum significantly upregulated IDE expression and downregulated APP and BACE levels, leading to reduced intracellular and extracellular Aβ accumulation. Furthermore, Naofucong suppressed excessive phosphorylation of ERK, JNK, and p38 in the MAPK pathway, an effect that was consistent with that observed following TZ intervention. These findings suggest that Naofucong mitigates Aβ deposition, at least in part, by enhancing IDE-associated Aβ degradation and suppressing BACE-associated Aβ production. This dual regulatory effect may be associated with inhibition of the MAPK signaling pathway, as supported by pharmacological blockade using TZ, highlighting a multi-target mechanism of Naofucong in Aβ-associated cognitive impairment.

Title: Carbonyl stress as the missing molecular link between diabetes and neurodegeneration: a unified mechanistic framework for type 3 diabetes.
Original_Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with an increased risk of cognitive dysfunction and neurodegenerative changes, contributing to the emerging concept of "Type 3 Diabetes," characterized by impaired cerebral insulin signaling and altered brain glucose metabolism. However, the metabolic processes connecting systemic metabolic dysfunction with cerebral insulin resistance remain incompletely understood. This review examines carbonyl stress, particularly methylglyoxal and other reactive dicarbonyls, as potential links between dysregulated glucose metabolism and impaired cerebral insulin signaling. We evaluate MGO generation and glyoxalase-mediated detoxification, evidence linking carbonyl stress with insulin-signaling abnormalities and interactions among AGE-RAGE signaling, oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing evidence from peripheral insulin-responsive tissues, vascular compartments and neuronal models, given the limited direct in vivo evidence establishing MGO as a cause of cerebral insulin resistance. The review further considers potential consequences for neuronal metabolism, synaptic function, and neurodegenerative vulnerability, alongside emerging therapeutic strategies targeting carbonyl metabolism and related pathways, including intranasal nanocarrier-mediated delivery. Overall, carbonyl stress represents a biologically plausible but not yet established molecular link between diabetes-associated metabolic dysfunction and neurodegenerative vulnerability, warranting brain-specific studies to determine its causal and therapeutic relevance.

Title: The obesity-neuroinflammation-cancer axis: neuroimmune remodeling and therapeutic opportunities.
Original_Abstract: Obesity is a chronic metabolic and inflammatory disorder associated with increased risk and poorer outcomes in multiple malignancies. Although adipose inflammation, insulin resistance, and altered adipokine signaling are established links between obesity and cancer, these mechanisms do not fully explain how systemic metabolic stress is translated into persistent changes in tissue immunity and tumor behavior. This narrative Review proposes the obesity-neuroinflammation-cancer axis as an integrative framework in which obesity-associated metabolic and inflammatory signals perturb central and peripheral neural homeostasis, while neuroinflammation, neural remodeling, and neuroendocrine signaling reshape the tumor microenvironment through reciprocal interactions among nerves, immune cells, stromal cells, and cancer cells. We focus on obesity-induced neuroinflammation, tumor neuroimmune remodeling, and neuroimmunometabolic feedback, highlighting sympathetic signaling, leptin-JAK/STAT3, NF-κB, inflammasome pathways, and metabolic reprogramming. We further evaluate therapeutic opportunities involving metabolic, inflammatory, and adrenergic interventions, including their combination with immune checkpoint blockade, while emphasizing inconsistent clinical evidence and the need for composite biomarkers. This framework is intended as a testable synthesis rather than a universally established causal pathway and identifies cancer-type-specific neuroimmune circuits as a priority for future translational research.

Title: DHHC12 serves as a critical nutrient-responsive switch that couples amino acid sensing to insulin secretion.
Original_Abstract: Protein palmitoylation covalently attaches the energy metabolite palmitate to target proteins, yet how it is regulated by nutrient status remains elusive. Here, we identify the palmitoyltransferase DHHC12 as a critical nutrient-responsive switch, coupling amino acid availability to insulin secretion. Amino acid deficiency activates the kinase GCN2, which phosphorylates COPA at Thr777, enabling its function as an adaptor for the CRL4 E3 ligase complex and leading to ubiquitination of DHHC12 on two critical cysteine residues (Cys127 and Cys133, with Cys127 within the catalytic DHHC motif) and its subsequent degradation. In male mice, loss of Dhhc12 impairs insulin secretion and causes glucose intolerance. DHHC12 palmitoylates SYT7 to promote glucose-stimulated insulin exocytosis. The physiological relevance of this pathway is underscored by two human DHHC12 variants: the hypoglycemia-associated L196P mutant evades degradation, whereas the hyperglycemia-linked N238I mutant is constitutively degraded. Together, our findings establish the GCN2-COPA-DHHC12 axis as a direct nutrient-sensing mechanism that couples amino acid availability to systemic glucose homeostasis.

Title: Prospective molecular targets for the future of thyroid eye disease treatment.
Original_Abstract: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common orbital inflammatory disorder associated with autoimmune thyroid disease. Conventional anti-inflammatory treatment fails to address the heterogeneous clinical manifestations and is frequently associated with adverse events. These limitations underscore the need to identify robust molecular targets and develop mechanism-based precise treatment for TED. This review summarized the landscape of prospective molecular targets for TED treatment. We provided a concise overview of the molecular mechanisms in TED, which is initiated by abnormal activation of insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor and thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, and amplified by downstream inflammatory signaling. The discussion of emerging therapeutic molecular targets was then presented, which can be divided into four categories: blockade of disease-specific autoantibody response, modulation of pathogenic humoral immunity, inhibition of cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathway and mitigation of fibroblast-centered tissue remodeling. We elaborated on current major molecular targets and highlighted promising candidates that may facilitate the development of next-generation precision therapies. Advances in understanding TED pathogenesis have expanded the repertoire of promising molecular targets. Future therapeutic development should extend beyond the validation of novel molecular targets to incorporate biomarker-guided patient stratification, rational combination therapies, and optimized drug delivery systems, thereby improving the treatment efficacy.

Title: Panax notoginseng alleviates obesity and insulin resistance involving the Enterocloster clostridioformis-IRS-PI3K-AKT axis.
Original_Abstract: In this study, supplementation with Panax notoginseng (PN) in obese mice reversed excessive weight gain, improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, and significantly reversed hepatic steatosis. Concurrently, PN treatment normalized the intestinal microecosystem, reflected in a decreased Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio (F/B ratio) and an enrichment of the commensal species Enterocloster clostridioformis (EC). Of particular note, oral administration of EC alone largely reproduced the major beneficial phenotypes observed with PN-namely, reduced fat mass, improved glycaemic regulation, and attenuated hepatic triglyceride deposition. Mechanistically, EC intervention suppressed the pathological overactivation of the hepatic insulin receptor substrate (IRS)-phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase (PI3K)-AKT kinase (AKT) pathway and inhibited the phosphorylation of IRS. This recalibration of the insulin signaling cascade improved insulin sensitivity and effectively counteracted the metabolic disturbances provoked by the high-fat diet (HFD). Taken together, these results suggest that the anti-obesity effects of PN are at least partially mediated by gut microbiota-driven EC enrichment, with consequent modulation of the IRS-PI3K-AKT pathway. Collectively, our findings identify EC as a potential candidate commensal bacterium and highlight the importance of the PN-EC-IRS-PI3K-AKT regulatory axis in counteracting obesity and its associated comorbidities.

Title: MicroRNA-9-5p targets ELAVL1 to regulate NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cardiomyocyte pyroptosis in diabetic hypoglycemic myocardial injury.
Original_Abstract: Recurrent hypoglycemia during intensive glycemic control in diabetes is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its myocardial damage remain poorly understood. This study aimed to investigate the role of post-transcriptional regulatory networks in diabetic recurrent hypoglycemic myocardial injury. Type 2 diabetic mouse models were established using a high-fat diet combined with streptozotocin (STZ) injection, and recurrent hypoglycemia was induced by repeated insulin administration. Integrated mRNA-seq and small RNA-seq were performed to screen differentially expressed genes and microRNAs (miRNAs). Key upstream regulators of the NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome were identified via Pearson correlation analysis combined with predictions from the StarBase, TargetScan, and miRDB databases. Direct binding between miRNA and target gene was verified by dual-luciferase reporter assays. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were conducted in a diabetic hypoglycemic HL-1 cardiomyocyte model by transfection with miR-9-5p mimics/inhibitor and ELAV-like protein 1 (ELAVL1)-targeting short hairpin RNA (sh-ELAVL1). In vivo intervention and rescue experiments were performed via tail vein injection of miR-9-5p agomir/antagomir and sh-ELAVL1 lentivirus. Myocardial structure and function were evaluated using echocardiography, hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining, immunofluorescence, and Western blot. Mice with diabetic recurrent hypoglycemia exhibited significant weight loss (p < 0.001) and impaired cardiac function. Transcriptome analysis identified 42 differentially expressed genes between the diabetic (DM) and diabetic hypoglycemic (HDM) groups, with specific enrichment of the NOD-like receptor signaling pathway. Protein levels of NLRP3, cleaved caspase-1 (p20), and the N-terminal fragment of gasdermin D (GSDMD-N, p30) in the myocardium were further significantly upregulated in the HDM group compared with the DM group (p < 0.001). Correlation analysis combined with StarBase database screening identified ELAVL1 as the key upstream RNA-binding protein regulating NLRP3 (r = 0.82, p < 0.001). Small RNA sequencing revealed 16 significantly downregulated miRNAs in the HDM group versus the DM group. Intersection with TargetScan and miRDB predictions of ELAVL1-targeting miRNAs identified miR-9-5p as the sole candidate, which was significantly downregulated in the HDM group (p < 0.001). Dual-luciferase reporter assays confirmed direct binding of miR-9-5p to the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of ELAVL1 (p < 0.001). In vitro, transfection with miR-9-5p mimics significantly reduced the protein levels of ELAVL1, NLRP3, and cleaved caspase-1 (p < 0.001), increased cell viability, and decreased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release (p < 0.001). Conversely, miR-9-5p inhibitor promoted these pathological changes, which were fully reversed by sh-ELAVL1 (p < 0.001). In vivo, miR-9-5p agomir significantly improved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and left ventricular fractional shortening (LVFS) (both p < 0.01), inhibited co-localization of NLRP3 with apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC), and downregulated the protein levels of GSDMD-N, interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-18 (IL-18) (p < 0.001). miR-9-5p antagomir exacerbated these injuries, which were effectively reversed by co-administration of sh-ELAVL1 (p < 0.001). Our findings demonstrate that miR-9-5p directly targets ELAVL1 to inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation and cardiomyocyte pyroptosis, thereby attenuating myocardial injury and improving cardiac function in diabetic recurrent hypoglycemia. The miR-9-5p/ELAVL1/NLRP3 axis may represent a promising therapeutic target for diabetic hypoglycemic myocardial injury, although clinical validation of this axis in patients with diabetes remains to be performed.

Title: Constitutive PDGFRβ activation drives connective tissue overgrowth through STAT5-IGF1 signaling.
Original_Abstract: Autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations in platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta (PDGFRβ) cause overgrowth of the skeleton and other connective tissue in Kosaki overgrowth syndrome. However, the target cell type and signaling pathways underlying PDGFRβ-driven overgrowth are unknown. Normal postnatal growth is controlled by pituitary-secreted growth hormone (GH), which activates the STAT5 transcriptional factor to upregulate insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1). To investigate the role of the GH-STAT5-IGF1 pathway in PDGFRβ-related overgrowth, we generated mice with a PDGFRβ gain-of-function mutation in skeletal and fibroblast lineages, which resulted in STAT5 activation and gigantism. Conditional deletion of Stat5ab in connective tissue lineages rescued skeletal overgrowth and keloid-like fibrosis in the skin. Conditional deletion of GH receptor ( Ghr ) did not rescue overgrowth, indicating the physiological activator of STAT5 is not required for overgrowth. However, deletion of Igf1 , the STAT5 target gene, and its receptor, Igf1r , in connective tissue, rescued the overgrowth phenotype. These findings demonstrate a GHR-independent STAT5-IGF1 signaling pathway in mutant connective tissue cells, which mediates PDGFRβ-driven overgrowth in mice and potentially in humans with similar PDGFRB mutations.

Title: Conditioned media derived from HepG2 cells treated with phosphoeleganin synthetic-derived compound PE/2 improve cytokine balance and metabolic response in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
Original_Abstract: The liver-adipose axis regulates insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism, and its dysregulation contributes to metabolic disorders. PE/2, a semisynthetic derivative of the marine natural product phosphoeleganin, reduces IL-6 expression and secretion, enhancing insulin sensitivity in liver cells (HepG2). However, its role in liver-adipose communication is unclear. To clarify the impact of PE/2 on liver-adipose tissue crosstalk, the conditioned media approach was used. Protein and mRNA levels were analyzed by Western blot and Real-Time RT-PCR, respectively. Lipid and glucose metabolism were evaluated by Oil Red O staining and glucose consumption assays, respectively. Our results indicate that in 3T3-L1 adipocytes, conditioned media derived from PE/2-treated HepG2 cells (CMPE/2) increased adiponectin expression by 1.85-fold and reduced interleukin-8 and interleukin-1β mRNA levels by 43% and 52%, respectively, compared with conditioned media alone (CM). The protective adipokine phenotype induced by CMPE/2 was accompanied by 1.75-fold lipid accumulation and increased expression of adipogenic markers, including PPARγ, C/EBPα, GLUT4, and FABP4. To examine whether this profile translates into enhanced insulin sensitivity, we evaluated the insulin pathway. Interestingly, CM from insulin-stimulated HepG2 cells (CMIns) did not significantly increase insulin receptor (INSR) or Akt phosphorylation compared with CM from 3T3-L1 adipocytes. However, CM derived from HepG2 co-treated with insulin and PE/2 (CMIns+PE/2) increased INSR and Akt phosphorylation by 2.13- and 1.63-fold, respectively, compared to CM, and by 1.83- and 1.42-fold, respectively, compared to CMIns. Consistently, 3T3-L1 glucose consumption significantly improved in the presence of CMIns+PE/2. Treatment with the PI3K/Akt inhibitor LY294002 reversed the effects of CMIns+PE/2. Finally, supplementing recombinant IL-6 into CMPE/2-treated cells reduced the effect of this compound on the expression of inflammatory and adipogenic genes and on glucose consumption in 3T3-L1 adipocytes, corroborating the hypothesis that IL-6 is involved in the action mediated by PE/2. These findings suggest that PE/2 improves the metabolic-inflammatory profile in adipocytes by modulating hepatocyte-adipocyte crosstalk, highlighting its implication for metabolic dysfunctions associated with impaired liver-adipose communication.

Title: The WD40 domain of autophagy protein ATG-16.2 is required for lysosomal regulation and longevity in germline-less C. elegans.
Original_Abstract: Autophagy is a conserved cellular recycling pathway linked to longevity and regulated by autophagy-related (ATG) protein. Many of these proteins serve a key function in ATG8 lipidation onto autophagosomal membranes, a step that precedes subsequent lysosomal degradation. Recently, mammalian ATG16L1, a member of ATG8 lipidation machinery, have been shown to also direct ATG8 lipidation onto other membranes via its C-terminal WD40 domain in acutely stressed cells. However, whether such non-canonical functions of the ATG16L1 WD40 domain influence longevity remain largely unknown. Here, we endogenously deleted the WD40 domain of atg-16.2 , the C. elegans ortholog of ATG16L1 , and examined autophagy, healthspan and longevity. The ATG-16.2 WD40 domain was dispensable for healthspan measures and for ATG8 lipidation in whole animals and neurons but was required for autophagic flux across all major tissues examined. Notably, the ATG-16.2 WD40 domain was also critical in limiting lysosomal membrane damage after acute heat stress. Because long-lived C. elegans mutants are typically heat resistant, we asked whether this lysosomal function supported their thermotolerance and found the WD40 domain to be selectively required for thermotolerance induced by germline removal, but not by reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling or dietary restriction. In germline-less animals, loss of the ATG-16.2 WD40 domain reduced nuclear TFEB/HLH-30, reduced neuronal autophagic degradation, altered neuronal lysosomal pH, and sensitized animals to heat-induced lysosomal damage. Collectively, these findings establish the ATG16 WD40 domain as a regulator of autophagic degradation and lysosomal integrity in vivo, and show that this role is associated with longevity in a pathway-selective manner. The ATG-16.2 WD40 domain is dispensable for C. elegans healthspan but required for autophagic degradation in vivo The WD40 domain limits lysosomal membrane damage after acute heat stress in vivo The WD40 domain is selectively required for thermotolerance and longevity induced by germline removal ( glp-1/NotchR mutation) Elevated neuronal lysosomal pH in germline-less animals requires the WD40 domain.

Title: Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3β as a Central Regulator of Alzheimer's Disease: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Perspectives.
Original_Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurological condition marked by cognitive decline, memory impairment, extracellular amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation, and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs). Among the multiple molecular pathways involved in AD pathogenesis, glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) has emerged as a crucial signaling regulator due to its extensive contribution to neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Growing evidence suggests that abnormal activation of GSK-3β contributes not merely to classical AD hallmarks, including tau hyperphosphorylation and amyloidogenesis, but is also linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, autophagic impairment, ferroptosis, insulin resistance, and oxidative stress through modulation of the Nrf2 pathway. These findings place GSK-3β as a crucial molecular hub linking different pathogenic pathways in AD. This review outlines the structural attributes along with regulatory mechanisms of GSK-3β and extensively explores its involvement in AD pathophysiology. Specific emphasis is given to evolving mechanisms, such as metabolic dysregulation, ferroptosis, and antioxidant signaling pathways. Additionally, current breakthroughs in therapeutic targeting techniques such as ATP-competitive inhibitors, non-ATP-competitive inhibitors, allosteric modulators, natural chemicals, and clinically studied medicines are emphasized. The translational difficulties linked to selectivity, blood-brain barrier permeability, and clinical efficacies are also explored. Collectively, this review reinforces the therapeutic relevance of GSK-3β and indicates potential opportunities for creating effective disease-modifying therapies in AD.

Title: Multiscale and cross-organ antidiabetic effects of Ajuga decumbens and harpagide: Integrating hepatic metabolism, immune regulation, and gut microbiota.
Original_Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a complex metabolic disorder involving dysregulated glucose homeostasis and interconnected disturbances across multiple organs. Plant-derived bioactive compounds represent promising candidates for metabolic regulation. Although Ajuga decumbens exhibits anti-inflammatory and lipid-modulating activities, its antidiabetic potential and underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized, particularly from a multiscale and cross-organ perspective. This exploratory study aimed to evaluate the antidiabetic activities of A. decumbens extracts, identify candidate bioactive constituents, and investigate their potential mechanisms within an integrated multiscale framework. An integrated experimental strategy combining in vivo, in vitro, in silico, and omics-based approaches was employed. High-fat diet (HFD)-fed diabetic mice were used to evaluate acute and long-term metabolic effects. α-amylase inhibition assays were performed to investigate potential effects on carbohydrate digestion. Phytochemical profiling, quantitative chromatography, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to identify and characterize candidate bioactive constituents. Transcriptomic analysis and 16S rRNA gene sequencing were used to explore hepatic molecular responses and gut microbial alterations. Integrated correlation network analysis was subsequently performed to examine associations among metabolic phenotypes, hepatic gluconeogenic signaling, immune polarization, and gut microbiota. Ajuga decumbens leaf extract (ALE) reduced postprandial blood glucose by 27.77% following an acute starch challenge and inhibited α-amylase activity (IC₅₀ = 47.39 ± 8.84 μg/ml). Harpagide (HPG), identified as a quantitatively prominent bioactive constituent, also exhibited α-amylase inhibitory activity (IC₅₀ = 8.01 ± 1.48 μg/ml) and reduced postprandial glucose by 25.99%. Four weeks of treatment improved glycemic regulation, lipid metabolism, and insulin resistance-related indices while attenuating diabetes-associated histopathological abnormalities. Mechanistic investigations indicated that ALE and HPG modulated hepatic gluconeogenesis-associated signaling through the Akt/FoxO1 pathway and altered macrophage polarization-related markers. Both treatments were also associated with changes in gut microbial composition, including the relative abundances of an uncultured taxon within Desulfobacterota, Colidextribacter, and the Eubacterium xylanophilum group. Integrated correlation analysis further revealed two partially differentiated association networks linking hepatic gluconeogenic regulation, immune polarization, gut microbial composition and diversity, and metabolic phenotypes. These findings provide integrated evidence supporting the antidiabetic potential of A. decumbens leaf extract and HPG through multiple biological processes involving intestinal α-amylase inhibition, hepatic gluconeogenic regulation, immune modulation, and gut microbial alterations. The identification of distinct cross-scale association patterns provides a systematic framework for investigating their metabolic effects and supports further mechanistic and preclinical evaluation of ALE and HPG as plant-derived candidates for T2DM management.

Title: Combination of ezetimibe and sericin attenuates cadmium chloride-induced neurotoxicity in an experimental rat model by suppressing oxidative stress and neuroinflammation.
Original_Abstract: Cadmium chloride (CdCl<sub>2</sub>)-induced neurotoxicity is a global health concern, associated with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and downregulation of IGF-1R/GLP-1R/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling pathway. Agents targeting this pathway may offer a promising strategy to mitigate neurotoxic effects. Therefore, we proposed that ezetimibe, a lipid-lowering drug, and sericin, a natural silk protein with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, were evaluated for their potential to mitigate CdCl<sub>2</sub>-induced neurotoxicity in experimental rats. Seventy adult Wistar rats were allocated to receive control, CdCl<sub>2</sub> (5 mg/kg), CdCl<sub>2</sub> with ezetimibe (10 and 20 mg/kg), and sericin (200 and 400 mg/kg), or in combination for 28 days. Behavioral assessments, muscle coordination, and cognitive dysfunction were performed. Animals were sacrificed on day 29, and hippocampal tissue was used to perform oxidative stress markers, including malondialdehyde (MDA), nitrite, glutathione (GSH), estimation of acetylcholinesterase, and neurochemicals (serotonin, norepinephrine), neuroinflammatory markers, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1beta (IL-1β), nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), immunohistochemistry of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), mitochondrial complex-I activity, and protein expression of IGF-1R, GLP-1R, Nrf2, NF-κB, and HO-1. CdCl<sub>2</sub> exposure resulted in motor and cognitive deficits, increased oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Ezetimibe and sericin, specifically the combination group, showed more pronounced effects; they improved motor behavior, maintained redox homeostasis, restored neurotransmitter levels, reduced neuroinflammation, and increased mitochondrial complex-I activity. Moreover, they restored the protein expression of IGF-1R, GLP-1R, Nrf2, NF-κB, and HO-1. The results demonstrate that ezetimibe and sericin, alone and in combination, can counteract Cd<sup>2+</sup>-induced neurotoxicity.

Title: Microbiota-derived indole-3-propionic acid regulates glucose homeostasis via remodeling of hepatic mitochondrial metabolism.
Original_Abstract: The gut microbiota produces metabolites that circulate to host tissues and are increasingly linked to metabolic health, yet the mechanisms by which individual microbial products regulate liver glucose metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the tryptophan-derived microbial metabolite indole-3-propionic acid (IPA) as a direct modulator of hepatic glucose production. In primary hepatocytes, a focused screen of indole metabolites revealed that several indole-containing compounds suppress glucagon-stimulated glucose output, with IPA selected for further characterization. IPA selectively reduced glucose production from mitochondrial-dependent gluconeogenic substrates while largely preserving glycerol-supported glucose production, suggesting that it does not simply shut down gluconeogenesis but instead alters how hepatocytes use metabolic fuels. Mechanistic analyzes showed that IPA redirects lactate-derived carbon away from glucose production and reshapes mitochondrial metabolism, including redox balance, ATP availability, and urea cycle-linked metabolic activity. These effects occurred without detectable disruption of proximal insulin or glucagon signaling, supporting a model in which IPA acts primarily through intracellular metabolic remodeling. In mice, endogenous IPA levels varied with nutritional state, and short-term IPA administration improved fasting glycemia and glucose handling in Western diet-fed animals. Finally, microbiome-depleted mice colonized with IPA-producing Clostridium sporogenes displayed increased circulating IPA and improved glucose tolerance compared with mice colonized with an IPA-deficient mutant C. Sporogenes strain. Together, these findings identify IPA as a microbial metabolite that directly connects gut tryptophan metabolism to hepatic mitochondrial function and systemic glucose regulation, highlighting a mechanistic gut-liver pathway with potential therapeutic relevance to metabolic disease.

Title: Insight of the role of mitochondrial iron homeostasis in insulin resistance.
Original_Abstract: Insulin resistance (IR) is characterized by impaired insulin responsiveness in metabolic tissues, leading to defective glucose disposal, dysregulated lipid metabolism, and compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Mitochondrial iron homeostasis is crucial for cellular metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and redox balance. Dysregulation of mitochondrial iron contributes to IR by impairing electron transport chain (ETC) function, increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS), and disrupting insulin signaling pathways. Excess mitochondrial iron leads to oxidative stress through the Fenton reaction, promoting lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammation, all of which exacerbate metabolic disorders. Additionally, mitochondrial iron overload affects iron-sulfur (Fe-S) cluster biosynthesis, mitochondrial dynamics, and energy metabolism, further impairing glucose homeostasis. Emerging evidence suggests that mitochondrial iron dysregulation plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and metabolic syndrome. Future research should focus on the molecular mechanisms governing mitochondrial iron transport and utilization, as well as its interaction with key metabolic pathways, to better understand its role in disease progression and potential therapeutic implications.

Title: Ursolic acid as a multi-target therapeutic candidate in type 2 diabetes mellitus: a mechanistic and translational review.
Original_Abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is interconnected disturbances in insulin signaling, pancreatic β-cell function, redox and inflammatory homeostasis, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and signaling mediated by advanced glycation end-product (AGE) and their receptors (RAGE). Although available antidiabetic therapies provide substantial clinical benefit, progressive β-cell dysfunction, and diabetes-associated tissue injury remain important clinical challenges. Ursolic acid (UA), a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid, has demonstrated broad preclinical metabolic and organ-protective effects, but the supporting evidence remains fragmented across individual pathways and experimental models. This review provides as updated, T2DM focussed in vitro, animal and limited human evidence, integrating UA-specific findings across insulin receptor/PTP1B signaling, β-cell preservation, redox regulation, inflammation, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial homeostasis and AGE-RAGE-associated injury. A key contribution is to stratify the mechanistic evidence rather than treating all pathway associations as equivalent, distinguishing direct or intervention-supported findings from expression-level associations, computational predictions and effects that may occur secondarily to improvements in glycaemia, insulin sensitivity, adiposity or oxidative stress. The review focus is comparatively stronger for the insulin-sensitising, lipid-regulatory, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of UA, whereas direct AGE-RAGE modulation, circadian regulation and some pathway specific β-cell mechanisms remain preliminary. The translational development of UA is constrained by poor aqueous solubility, low oral bioavailability, uncertain dose exposure relationships, limited dose standardisation, insufficient long-term safety data, and lack of robust clinical validation in patients with T2DM. UA represents a multi-target preclinical candidate, rather than a clinically established antidiabetic therapy. Future research should prioritise pathway-specific validation, standardized diabetes-relevant models, pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic correlation, controlled clinical studies, and long-term safety assessment.
